newsitem.title: HAITI: New opposition to foreign occupation in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: New opposition to foreign occupation in Haiti.

text.p: Haitians are voicing new opposition to the continued presence of foreign troops as the date approaches for a U.N. peacekeeping force to leave the country or extend its mandate again.

Haiti's U.N. representative Enrique Ter Horst said this month a third extension of the peacekeeping mandate would be "useful" beyond the scheduled Nov. 30 U.N. pullout. But while Haitians rejoiced when 20,000 U.S. troops arrived in Sept. 1994 to restore President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power after three years of murderous military dictatorship, some now say their guests have stayed too long.

President Rene Preval, who came to power in elections held since the intervention, has not yet requested or commented on the possibility of an extension. U.N. spokesman Eric Falt also declined to comment.

The arrival on Wednesday of a contingent of 15 U.S. police officers to join a U.N. police training unit and even the fact that Canadian soldiers have arranged to keep renting pool tables from local bars suggest foreign troops plan to stay. But oppopsition to an extension has emerged in Parliament.

"We believe we are about at the time where the foreign troops can go home so that the political power can take on its total mission, particularly its mission of sovereignty," Senate President Edgar LeBlanc said recently.

A group called the Committee Against Foreign Organisation has been circulating a petition against renewal of the mandate and some parliamentarians who say they support an extension say it should be requested only under new terms.
"I think the peacekeeping soldiers could be more active," Deputy Alix Fils-Aime said. "I think they could be more involved in civic action, building infrastructure, more work training the police."
He said those who wanted a pullout were subversive elements seeking to destablize the government.

The capabilty of the newly formed Haitian National Police force is at the centre of any decision about when peacekeeping troops can leave. Dozens of police officers allegedly involved in crimes ranging from torture to theft have been purged and trainers say improvements have been made.

Civilian Mission in Haiti (MICIVIH) chief Colin Grandeson, who has been tracking the police's human rights record, has applauded a strenghtening of the Inspector General's office, which works as an internal affairs bureau for the police.
"The mechanisms have been put in place and at the moment are working," he said.

Those who support an extension say the police are not yet equipped to deter subversives such as those who attacked the Port-au-Prince police station in August with grenades. Police trainers said officers at the station ran away during the attack.

Even if the 1,600 U.N. troops in Haiti were to leave, 300 soldiers would stay behind in the U.S. Support Group, now comprised largely of engineers. The group also has a Psychological Operations team which has been working with police in a public relations campaign.
Small units of U.S. Marines and soldiers, officially brought in for training exercises but also seen patrolling, have also been brought in monthly.

U.S. Defence Department diplomatic security agents moved into the Presidential Palace after suspicions that members of Preval's security team were involved in the August assassinations of two opposition politicians.
The shake-up of palace security was widely viewed as an attempt by the Clinton administration to maintain Haiti as a foreign policy success story in his presidential campaign.
